title: Rapid SDK Environment Hypothesis Lab Notebook
content:
OVERVIEW

This notebook captures a compact, experiment-first plan for a developer SDK environment quickstart that favors hypothesis-driven micro-experiments over long prescriptive guides. Goal: deliver a 7-minute reproducible developer experience that demonstrates end-to-end flow (auth -> sample request -> local fallback) and surfaces predictable failure modes with telemetry hooks.

PROBLEM STATEMENT
- Current quickstarts are text-heavy and assume an interactive UI. New users want a reproducible CLI flow and a one-file sample app (node/python) that runs with minimal setup.
- We need to validate which minimal steps remove the largest friction for first-time SDK users.

PRIMARY HYPOTHESES (ranked)
1) A single runnable sample (no install beyond language runtime + one tiny script) reduces time-to-first-success by 60% compared to a multi-file repo.
2) Shipping an intentionally small failure (token auth expired or missing env var) with clear remediation text increases user recovery rate in the first session by 3x.
3) Embedding one telemetry assert (latency < 200ms sample) in the quickstart gives teams immediate confidence about runtime performance and surfaces early infra bugs.

EXPERIMENTS (micro-runs)
Experiment A: One-file sample app (node + fetch)
- Create a single file `quickstart.js` that: reads REDWOOD_API_KEY from env, calls the hosted API with a 20-token prompt, prints streaming text, exits.
- Success metric: 70% of internal test users get valid output within 7 minutes (measured via lab session poll).
- Failure injection: if API key missing, print exact remediation steps and provide `--demo` mode that uses a short stubbed sample response.

Experiment B: Intentional auth failure flow
- Provide a CLI flag `--simulate-expired-key` that reproduces the expired token error and prints the remediation link.
- Success metric: percentage of users who fix the issue without raising a support ticket.

Experiment C: Telemetry assertion and smoke metric
- Quickstart emits a single event to the sandbox telemetry endpoint with fields: sample_id, elapsed_ms, success|fail.
- Predicate: show the elapsed_ms in the console and fail the quickstart with a friendly message if latency > 2000ms.

QUICKSTART OUTLINE (developer path - 7 minutes)
1) Clone or curl a single file: curl -fsSL https://dl.redwood.ai/quickstarts/onefile > quickstart.js
2) Set env: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="sk-..." (or run: quickstart.js --demo)
3) Run: node quickstart.js
4) Observe streaming output, telemetry line, and guidance if an error occurred.

SAMPLE CONSOLE OUTPUT (illustrative)
> Starting Redwood quickstart (onefile)
> Using API key: REDACTED
> Streaming response: Hello! I can help with...
> Telemetry: sample_id=lab-20241106 elapsed_ms=180 success
> Next steps: try the SDK with a full sample app: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-starter

SMOKE TESTS AND FAILURE MODES (to include in CI)
- Missing key -> prints remediation and `--demo` hint (should exit code 1).
- Invalid key -> prints link to account page and shows masked key with note to rotate.
- Network timeout -> retry backoff shown; provide `--offline` stub mode for demos.
- Streaming aborted -> fall back to non-streaming single-request call.

TELEMETRY & METRICS (minimal)
- Events: quickstart.launch, quickstart.success, quickstart.failure, quickstart.latency_ms (values).
- Goal: instrument in a way that doesn't require user opt-in for the lab environment (sandbox only).
- Dashboard: internal devexp dashboard panel for adoption funnel (launch -> success -> follow-on repo clone).

CONTENT & DOC TONE
- Keep doc text bite-sized; prefer in-console remediation and a follow-up short web page with deeper troubleshooting.
- Include a short checklist for integrators and SEs so they can reproduce customer issues quickly.

ROLL-OUT STRATEGY
Phase 0 (this lab): build the one-file quickstart + telemetry + failure injection. Run an internal adoption lab with 20 engineers (goal: 15/20 success within 7 minutes).
Phase 1: iterate based on lab results; build language variants (python, go) once the node path stabilizes.
Phase 2: promote to public quickstart, add a tiny GitHub repo (single-file + README + 3-line test) and link from docs.redwood.ai.

CHECKLIST FOR IMPLEMENTATION (owner: Priya)
- [ ] Write quickstart onefile (node) with `--demo`, `--simulate-expired-key`, `--offline` flags. (ETA: 1 week)
- [ ] Add telemetry hooks and internal sandbox endpoint. (ETA: 3 days)
- [ ] Draft minimal web troubleshooting doc (1 page). (ETA: 3 days)
- [ ] Run internal lab session and collect metrics. (ETA: 1 week after prototype)
- [ ] Iterate and prepare language variants.

OPEN QUESTIONS / DECISIONS NEEDED
- Opt-in vs. opt-out telemetry: for sandbox it's fine to emit minimal telemetry, but public quickstart requires clear privacy copy. (Action: legal review)
- Do we pin quickstart to a specific SDK version or to the hosted API? Pinning makes debugging easier but increases maintenance cost. (Action: propose policy)

LINKS / REFERENCES
- Confluence: DEVEXP quickstarts index: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DEVEXP/Quickstarts
- GitHub starter seed: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-starter
- Jira epic: JIRA-DEVEXP-456

NOTES TO SELF (brain dump)
- Keep examples < 40 lines. Users skip long READMEs.
- Invest in console-level UX: one or two clear lines that tell the user what to do next.

NEXT STEPS
- Build prototype and schedule 2 internal lab runs next week. Capture time-to-first-success metric and number of support escalations.
- Follow up with SEs and Solutions team for common friction capture.

END
